events.text:
The Department of War, in coordination with Lockheed Martin and European allies, has selected Poland to host a European PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, the Pentagon announced October 27th, on the margins of NATO’s Conference of National Armaments Directors. Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden will lead supply chain integration, according to the release. 
PAC-3 is the interceptor missile fired by Patriot air defense systems. The facility will conduct maintenance, repair and overhaul in Europe. It is not for building new missiles. The Pentagon says doing that work in the region will “dramatically shorten turnaround times” and give allies surge capacity in a crisis, but does not quantify either. Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey said allies are investing national resources “to establish this critical sustainment capability on NATO’s Eastern Front.”
The decision follows a July 7th agreement, signed at the NATO summit in Ankara by the U.S., Germany, the Netherlands, Poland and Sweden, to explore such a facility. Lockheed Martin said at the time it would support allies operating both PAC-3 MSE and PAC-3 Cost Reduction Initiative interceptors.
Source: https://www.war.gov/News/Releases/Release/Article/4634407/poland-selected-to-host-historic-pac-3-missile-maintenance-facility-strengtheni/

🇬🇧 King Charles heads to the Caribbean as colonial wounds remain open
 
King Charles III and Queen Camilla begin a nine-day Caribbean tour on October 27, visiting the Bahamas and Guyana before the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, as former British colonies intensify demands for Britain to confront slavery’s legacy.
 
With Buckingham Palace earlier ruling out a formal apology, Caribbean leaders are currently pressing Britain on several fronts:
 
🟥 Reparations: CARICOM, a regional bloc representing Caribbean countries, wants reparations on the Commonwealth summit agenda, from financial compensation to the return of cultural artifacts
🟥 Political independence: The Bahamas remains a constitutional monarchy despite gaining independence in 1973, while Jamaica pursues reparations and moves towards becoming a republic
🟥 Indigenous rights: In Guyana, community leaders raise concerns over land disputes and their lack of representation in decisions affecting their communities
 
For some, the visit raises a deeper question: why does the British monarch still hold such a prominent place in the region? “Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us?” asked Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
 
CARICOM Secretary-General Carla Barnett, meanwhile, described reparations as something that is “fundamentally about justice” and building “a just and equitable future” for descendants of those who endured colonial enslavement.

🇮🇱 Israel's elections unlikely to change course on Gaza and Iran
Israel's opposition says it will offer an alternative to Benjamin Netanyahu, but big changes in policy toward Gaza and Iran seem unlikely no matter who wins the elections, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who is now a top Netanyahu rival, helped create the Dahiya Doctrine, which calls for using overwhelming force against militant strongholds. He also sat in Netanyahu's war cabinet and has raised doubts about whether regime change in Iran is possible, instead of rejecting military action outright.
Another opposition leader, Naftali Bennett, has rejected concessions to Palestinians. Meanwhile, polls show growing right-wing sentiment among Jewish Israelis and continued support for an Israeli military presence in Gaza and Lebanon.
Analysts say opposition candidates must appeal to Netanyahu’s right-wing voters to win, leaving little room for a major shift in security policy.

events.text:
💵 Lockheed Martin bags $694M contract to build hypersonic missile - report
Despite a record of failed flight tests that nearly killed the program in 2023, the US Air Force has awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract to move the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW) beyond prototyping and into production, Stars and Stripes reports.
With a range of 1,000 miles and speeds exceeding Mach 5, the boost-glide missile destroys its target on impact using kinetic energy. Testing has mainly involved the B-52H, with the B-1B also slated for future use. The deal was signed on September 29 under the Pentagon’s Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract model — a fast-track mechanism that bypasses the usual oversight.
Even with the new contract in hand, the Pentagon has not disclosed how many missiles it will buy or when they will enter service — leaving Washington’s long-running hypersonic ambitions facing another test: turning years of development and spending into a deployable weapon.
In October, the US Army confirmed that the country is running more than three years behind schedule in fielding its first hypersonic weapons system, Dark Eagle. Lockheed has burned through billions of dollars on programs that repeatedly miss their deadlines — while the Pentagon keeps writing the checks.
